en: When she saw noble Buurul,
Your precious mother Aichürök
Had fallen down as though dead.
Aichürök stood shrieking,
Seytek sobbed and wept,
The speechless horse Buurul wept,
Everyone who beheld them wept,
The people watching wept,
The broad-breasted earth itself wept.
His face went pale and wan,
And the tears flowing from both eyes
Poured down over his chest.
They gathered all along the cliffside camp,
As if the colossal, mountain-like lion
Had only just died.
Their bellies churned and their souls burned,
Their bodies went limp and their blood burned;
The world closed in around them,
And anguish smoldered within.
As though the bloodthirsty gray-maned hero had died,
As though they had seen calamity that very day,
They sobbed and wept, yet could not die,
Unable to take their own lives.
Snot streamed from their noses like spring water,
And they rode on, weeping convulsively,
Standing there bereft of strength,
Their thoughts utterly distracted.
The gray-maned hero’s Buurul
Appeared before his eyes exactly like
His lion-hearted father Semetey.
Every joint trembled and gave way,
And the orphan wailed in anguish.
To the lion-hearted son of his father,
His father’s heavenly steed,
Noble Buurul, appeared before him,
And when the orphan saw him,
Tears poured from his eyes.
He wished to die, yet could not die.
Have I taken your piebald horse?
Have I chased away your wild ass?
You swaggering caravan men,
Have I scattered the money from your saddlebags?
You began this wrongdoing yourselves,
You blustering caravan men;
Now see what sport you will get from me!
You say, “Give us your bundled money,”
And, “Obey what we say at once.”
Which of you have I wronged?
I have committed no offense today;
You sixty mighty caravan men,
Why have you provoked my anger?
When did I ever enrage you
By demanding half your money?
My wrath is rising; I stand unyielding,
I will not spare a single one of you.
Why did you rouse my fury?
You have sorely offended my spirit;
I let it pass unnoticed, caravan men.
You are turning this into an ugly quarrel;
If I simply leave you to yourselves,
You strike people with cast-iron maces.
All sixty of you band together,
Halting wherever you please,
And cursing mothers and daughters.
You have gone rabid, you unruly caravan men,
Swaggering in your insolence.
Refusing to leave peaceful people alone,
Why have you provoked my anger?
My wrath is rising; I stand unyielding;
Now I will not leave
A single one of you untouched!
I will plunder your livestock,
Cut short every one of your lives,
And, as though a terrible slaughter had struck,
Destroy you all!
You blustering caravan men,
Your guilt is upon your own heads,
And your punishment upon your black crowns!”
His courage was as hard as his loins.
To hear his battle cry,
It was like an icy gorge wind.
If left alone, he would finish them utterly,
And reclaim
The aged Buurul.
Scraggly-bearded Karasart
Stood ready at the very front;
The thickset, vulture-tailed caravan man,
That ill-fated wretch,
Had armed himself for the attack.
The sixty mighty caravan men
Spread out with grim faces,
Their hostile intent plain to see.
They rushed forward, striking in a frenzy,
Speaking the vilest words.
A cast-iron mace as thick as a house post
Whirled past in his grip
And reached brave Seytek.
A knobbed mace and battle-axe—
He gripped it in both hands and swung it,
Then hurled the blow at noble Seytek
The moment he came within reach.
One blow did not kill him;
His father, the peerless gray-maned hero,
Had counted such a blow no more than a fly.
His anger flared and his eyes widened.
Burning fiercely as he mourned his father,
Finding no dust vast enough to scatter,
No blood enough to swallow,
No mountain great enough to set right,
No enemy enough to exhaust his rage upon,
Grim-faced brave Seytek
Struck his dark-bay horse upon the flank,
Took tempered steel in hand,
Broke through the barrier and opened a path.
The falcon thundered without pause
And attacked the caravan men.
“To your fathers’ graves, caravan men!
Have I reaped your grain before it ripened?
When Seytek launched his attack,
The strongmen stood aghast;
The strongmen who had come blustering
Lay stretched out dead.
Not one champion stood his ground or escaped;
The sixty mighty caravan men
Were annihilated then and there.
They had assailed the lion-hearted hero,
And the strongmen at the front froze,
Entangling themselves in their own deaths.
By assailing the renowned lion,
They had ensnared themselves in disaster.
Their bundled money lay in a heap,
And with that, alas,
The sixty strongmen were no more.
He wrought a terrible slaughter;
Not leaving a single one,
He struck off their heads with his sword.
Your divinely favored falcon
Did not leave so much as a hair,
But massacred them all.
Silks and money piled up,
And every one of the strongmen was slain.
His fortune had turned full,
And a hero upheld by divine favor arose;
His eyelashes became tongues of flame,
And against the leopard hero’s son
No one had a word of defiance left.
His father’s inheritance,
Noble Buurul, had been found,
And the father’s son, alas,
Recovered his honor through this deed.
The strongmen who had challenged him
Had wielded strength surpassing all others,
Yet your hero’s fury
Proved mightier than them all.
By providence he encountered
His father the khan’s noble steed,
Found upon the road as he journeyed.
Before he could turn the stallion’s head,
Once brave Seytek had spoken these words,
His eyes blazed like a lion’s.
His bloodlust seized him,
And strength and power surged through his body;
From the fire of his two cheeks,
Hair a sock’s length seemed to spring.
Would he spare those he encountered?
Would the tiger hero’s offspring,
On meeting foes, not gorge himself on blood?
Would he spare those who grappled with him?
Would the leopard’s offspring,
When attacked, not glut himself with blood?
He snatched up the golden-cheeked battle-axe
And swung it round;
At Karasart, the caravan chief,
He brought it down upon the crown.
Karasart, head of the caravan,
Was struck by the young warrior’s axe.
His head flew off with a crash,
His life fled with a shriek.
When the sixty mighty caravan men
Saw that battle,
Courage drained from their hearts
And strength from their wrists;
Their eyes bulged in panic.
The sixty mighty caravan men,
Their tiny souls shrieking,
Scattered and fled in every direction.
Would he spare a fleeing foe?
If he did not attack the foe who challenged him,
How could the leopard Seytek prosper?
He took Joybolot in hand,
Struck his dark-bay horse upon the flank,
Raised a cry like brave Manas,
And charged the caravan men,
Striking them down as if in sport.
Ten died where he played,
Others died facing him at the ridge,
And five or six of them, if you looked,
Died where they had fought so fiercely before.
For blood-red slaughter and battle,
The noble steed was perfectly fitted.
In grievous, desperate conflict,
The noble steed had stood firm.
When given barley, he crunched it,
His eyes shining like an argali’s;
He cracked wheat between his teeth,
His eyes shining like a stag’s.
When ridden into battle, he never flinched,
The blessed, broad-chested courser.
Through heat that seemed to burn the brain,
Through stench reeking of dung,
Across forty-one high mountain passes,
Across deserts forty days wide,
You were a beast that endured it all,
For you possessed the nature of a tulpar.
You were a soul dearer than a father.”
So Külchoro lamented,
Grasping the forelock and breathing in its scent,
Sniffing him deeply, saying, “My inherited Buurul.”
His reason fled and his heart burned,
His heart aflame with grief.
Having found the camel-like gray steed,
He sobbed and wept all the harder.
God forbid anyone should behold it:
When he saw Külchoro,
The noble steed, massive as a camel,
Neighed and snorted,
Pawed and pounded the black earth,
Flung his forelock toward the sky,
And hammered the ground with his hooves.
He clattered his bit,
And strained, dragging at the earth;
Noble Buurul stood leaning close,
And Taybuurul kept sniffing
At Külchoro’s neck.
His mane and tail streamed apart;
The animal heaved deep sighs,
And tears poured from his eyes.
As Buurul stood weeping,
His noble elder brother Külchoro,
Before he could cry out the glad tidings,
Külchoro, upheld by divine favor,
Saw Buurul before his eyes,
And tears poured from them.
He pressed his face to noble Buurul’s forelock,
Breathing in its scent,
Clasped him and sniffed him deeply,
Saying, “You remain to me from my father.”
Though he was a beast, he had a soul;
Your swift horse was a trusted companion,
An inheritance left behind
By my gray-maned father, Khan Manas.
We came together when I was no bigger than a louse,
We joined as one when I was no bigger than a thumb;
He carried me across ravines,
Guarding me like a father,
A peerless steed renowned among the people,
